sections.normalized_html: A soccer ball is kicked straight upward. It reaches a maximum height of [MATH: 48] feet at [MATH: 2] seconds and hits the ground at [MATH: 4] seconds. Which equation represents the height above ground [MATH: H,] in feet, of the soccer ball [MATH: t] seconds after it is kicked?
sections.readable_text: A soccer ball is kicked straight upward. It reaches a maximum height of [MATH: 48] feet at [MATH: 2] seconds and hits the ground at [MATH: 4] seconds. Which equation represents the height above ground [MATH: H,] in feet, of the soccer ball [MATH: t] seconds after it is kicked?

sections.normalized_html:
We can model the motion of the soccer ball with a downward-opening quadratic function whose vertex (maximum point) is [MATH: (h, k)], in vertex form:

[MATH: H(t) = a(t - h)^2 + k]

First, we know the ball reached its maximum height of [MATH: 48] feet after [MATH: 2] seconds. This means the vertex of the quadratic function is at [MATH: (2, 48),] so [MATH: h = 2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad k = 48.]

Next, we know the ball returned to the ground level at [MATH: t = 4,] so [MATH: H(4) = 0.] So we set up the equation and solve for [MATH: a{:}]

[MATH: H(4)|= a(4 − 2)^{2} + 48; 0|= a(2)^{2} + 48; 0|= 4a + 48; − 4a|= 48; a|= − (48)/(4); a|= − 12]

So the height equation is

[MATH: H(t) = -12(t - 2)^2 + 48.]

Therefore, rewriting it in standard form, the equation that represents the height of the soccer ball above the ground [MATH: t] seconds after it is kicked is

[MATH: H(t)|= − 12(t − 2)^{2} + 48; = − 12(t^{2} − 4t + 4) + 48; = − 12t^{2} + 48t − 48 + 48; = − 12t^{2} + 48t.]

sections.normalized_html: The quadratic function [MATH: D] models the depth, in meters, below the surface of the water of a research vessel’s tethered camera [MATH: t] minutes after it was lowered. The function estimates that the camera reached its maximum depth of [MATH: 225] meters [MATH: 4] minutes after it was lowered and then reached the surface of the water [MATH: 10] minutes after it was lowered. Based on the function, what was the estimated depth, to the nearest meter, of the camera [MATH: 6] minutes after it was lowered?
sections.readable_text: The quadratic function [MATH: D] models the depth, in meters, below the surface of the water of a research vessel’s tethered camera [MATH: t] minutes after it was lowered. The function estimates that the camera reached its maximum depth of [MATH: 225] meters [MATH: 4] minutes after it was lowered and then reached the surface of the water [MATH: 10] minutes after it was lowered. Based on the function, what was the estimated depth, to the nearest meter, of the camera [MATH: 6] minutes after it was lowered?

sections.normalized_html:
We model the depth of the camera below the water’s surface with a quadratic function [MATH: D(t),] where [MATH: t] is the number of minutes since it was lowered and [MATH: D(t)] gives the depth in meters. Since the camera reaches a maximum depth, the function takes the vertex form: [MATH: D(t) = a(t - h)^2 + k] where [MATH: (h, k)] is the vertex of the parabola.

First, we know the camera reached its maximum depth of [MATH: 225] meters after [MATH: 4] minutes. This means the vertex of the quadratic function is at [MATH: (4, 225)], so [MATH: h = 4 \qquad\text{and}\qquad k = 225.]

Next, we know the camera reached the surface of the water ([MATH: 0] depth) at [MATH: t = 10,] which means [MATH: D(10) = 0.] So we set up the equation and solve for [MATH: a{:}] [MATH: D(10)|= a(10 − 4)^{2} + 225; 0|= a(6)^{2} + 225; 0|= 36a + 225; − 36a|= 225; a|= − (225)/(36); a|= − (25)/(4)]

So the depth function is [MATH: D(t) = -\frac{25}{4}(t - 4)^2 + 225.]

Therefore, the depth at [MATH: t=6] is [MATH: D(6)|= − (25)/(4)(6 − 4)^{2} + 225; = − (25)/(4)(2)^{2} + 225; = − (25)/(4)(4) + 225; = − 25 + 225; = 200meters.]

sections.normalized_html: A skier launches off a ramp into the air. Her height, in meters above the ground, is modeled by a quadratic function of the time, in seconds, since she left the ramp. According to the model, she launched from a height of [MATH: 8] meters above the ground and reached her highest point of [MATH: 17] meters after [MATH: 3] seconds. After how many seconds does the model predict she will land? (Round to the nearest whole number)

According to the model, she launched from a height of [MATH: 8] meters above the ground and reached her highest point of [MATH: 17] meters after [MATH: 3] seconds. After how many seconds does the model predict she will land? (Round to the nearest whole number)

sections.normalized_html:
We can model the height of the skier above the ground with a downward-opening quadratic function whose vertex (maximum point) is [MATH: (h, k)], in vertex form: [MATH: h(t) = a(t - h)^2 + k]

First, we know the skier reached her maximum height of [MATH: 17] meters after [MATH: 3] seconds. This means the vertex of the quadratic function is at [MATH: (3, 17),] so [MATH: h = 3 \qquad\text{and}\qquad k = 17.]

Next, we know the skier launched from a height of [MATH: 8] meters at [MATH: t = 0,] which means [MATH: h(0) = 8.] So we set up the equation and solve for [MATH: a{:}] [MATH: h(0)|= a(0 − 3)^{2} + 17; 8|= a(3)^{2} + 17; 8|= 9a + 17; − 9a|= 17 − 8; − 9a|= 9; a|= − 1]

So the height function is [MATH: h(t) = -1(t - 3)^2 + 17.]

Now, to determine when the skier lands (zero height), we set up the equation [MATH: h(t) = 0] and solve for [MATH: t{:}] [MATH: h(t)|= − 1(t − 3)^{2} + 17; 0|= − 1(t − 3)^{2} + 17; (t − 3)^{2}|= 17; t − 3|= ± sqrt(17); t|= 3 ± sqrt(17)]

Evaluating, we find that the roots are

[MATH: t\approx -1.123, \qquad t\approx 7.1234.]

Since [MATH: t > 0,] we discard the negative option. Therefore, we have [MATH: t\approx 7.1234,] and rounding this to the nearest second gives [MATH: t = 7] seconds.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When presented with real-world data on vertical motion, we can often fit it to a quadratic model using vertex form. In this topic, we'll practice doing just that.

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing Quadratic Functions Given Data

Example Prompt:
A soccer ball is kicked straight upward. It reaches a maximum height of [MATH: 48] feet at [MATH: 2] seconds and hits the ground at [MATH: 4] seconds. Which equation represents the height above ground [MATH: H,] in feet, of the soccer ball [MATH: t] seconds after it is kicked?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can model the motion of the soccer ball with a downward-opening quadratic function whose vertex (maximum point) is [MATH: (h, k)], in vertex form:

[MATH: H(t) = a(t - h)^2 + k]

First, we know the ball reached its maximum height of [MATH: 48] feet after [MATH: 2] seconds. This means the vertex of the quadratic function is at [MATH: (2, 48),] so
[MATH: h = 2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad k = 48.]

Next, we know the ball returned to the ground level at [MATH: t = 4,] so [MATH: H(4) = 0.] So we set up the equation and solve for [MATH: a{:}]

[MATH: H(4)|= a(4 − 2)^{2} + 48; 0|= a(2)^{2} + 48; 0|= 4a + 48; − 4a|= 48; a|= − (48)/(4); a|= − 12]

So the height equation is

[MATH: H(t) = -12(t - 2)^2 + 48.]

Therefore, rewriting it in standard form, the equation that represents the height of the soccer ball above the ground [MATH: t] seconds after it is kicked is

[MATH: H(t)|= − 12(t − 2)^{2} + 48; = − 12(t^{2} − 4t + 4) + 48; = − 12t^{2} + 48t − 48 + 48; = − 12t^{2} + 48t.]

Item 5 — Example: Constructing and Evaluating Quadratic Functions Given Data

Example Prompt:
The quadratic function [MATH: D] models the depth, in meters, below the surface of the water of a research vessel’s tethered camera [MATH: t] minutes after it was lowered. The function estimates that the camera reached its maximum depth of [MATH: 225] meters [MATH: 4] minutes after it was lowered and then reached the surface of the water [MATH: 10] minutes after it was lowered. Based on the function, what was the estimated depth, to the nearest meter, of the camera [MATH: 6] minutes after it was lowered?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We model the depth of the camera below the water’s surface with a quadratic function [MATH: D(t),] where [MATH: t] is the number of minutes since it was lowered and [MATH: D(t)] gives the depth in meters. Since the camera reaches a maximum depth, the function takes the vertex form:
[MATH: D(t) = a(t - h)^2 + k]
where [MATH: (h, k)] is the vertex of the parabola.

First, we know the camera reached its maximum depth of [MATH: 225] meters after [MATH: 4] minutes. This means the vertex of the quadratic function is at [MATH: (4, 225)], so
[MATH: h = 4 \qquad\text{and}\qquad k = 225.]

Next, we know the camera reached the surface of the water ([MATH: 0] depth) at [MATH: t = 10,] which means [MATH: D(10) = 0.] So we set up the equation and solve for [MATH: a{:}]
[MATH: D(10)|= a(10 − 4)^{2} + 225; 0|= a(6)^{2} + 225; 0|= 36a + 225; − 36a|= 225; a|= − (225)/(36); a|= − (25)/(4)]

So the depth function is
[MATH: D(t) = -\frac{25}{4}(t - 4)^2 + 225.]

Therefore, the depth at [MATH: t=6] is
[MATH: D(6)|= − (25)/(4)(6 − 4)^{2} + 225; = − (25)/(4)(2)^{2} + 225; = − (25)/(4)(4) + 225; = − 25 + 225; = 200meters.]

Item 8 — Example: Constructing a Quadratic Function and Determining Its Roots

Example Prompt:
A skier launches off a ramp into the air. Her height, in meters above the ground, is modeled by a quadratic function of the time, in seconds, since she left the ramp. According to the model, she launched from a height of [MATH: 8] meters above the ground and reached her highest point of [MATH: 17] meters after [MATH: 3] seconds. After how many seconds does the model predict she will land? (Round to the nearest whole number)

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can model the height of the skier above the ground with a downward-opening quadratic function whose vertex (maximum point) is [MATH: (h, k)], in vertex form:
[MATH: h(t) = a(t - h)^2 + k]

First, we know the skier reached her maximum height of [MATH: 17] meters after [MATH: 3] seconds. This means the vertex of the quadratic function is at [MATH: (3, 17),] so
[MATH: h = 3 \qquad\text{and}\qquad k = 17.]

Next, we know the skier launched from a height of [MATH: 8] meters at [MATH: t = 0,] which means [MATH: h(0) = 8.] So we set up the equation and solve for [MATH: a{:}]
[MATH: h(0)|= a(0 − 3)^{2} + 17; 8|= a(3)^{2} + 17; 8|= 9a + 17; − 9a|= 17 − 8; − 9a|= 9; a|= − 1]

So the height function is
[MATH: h(t) = -1(t - 3)^2 + 17.]

Now, to determine when the skier lands (zero height), we set up the equation [MATH: h(t) = 0] and solve for [MATH: t{:}]
[MATH: h(t)|= − 1(t − 3)^{2} + 17; 0|= − 1(t − 3)^{2} + 17; (t − 3)^{2}|= 17; t − 3|= ± sqrt(17); t|= 3 ± sqrt(17)]

Evaluating, we find that the roots are

[MATH: t\approx -1.123, \qquad t\approx 7.1234.]

Since [MATH: t > 0,] we discard the negative option. Therefore, we have
[MATH: t\approx 7.1234,]
and rounding this to the nearest second gives [MATH: t = 7] seconds.
